lines.text: You've heard of the Trojan Horse.
You've never heard what it cost the man who built it: ten years, every ship, every friend.
On the way home he met a giant with one eye, a witch who turned his men into pigs, and a monster with six heads on six long necks.
He went down among the dead and watched them crowd around a pit of blood.
And when he finally got home, he walked into his own house dressed as a beggar, with a bow, and a hundred men inside who wanted his wife.
He left Troy with twelve ships and about six hundred men, and he came home alone.
The sea took some of them, and the monsters took others.
But if you follow the story closely, you keep finding Odysseus himself at the start of every disaster.
So let's start at the beginning, with the horse.
For ten years the Greeks threw themselves at the walls of Troy, and for ten years the walls held.
Achilles was dead by then, along with most of the men worth anything.
The kings were tired of each other, and the ships were rotting on the beach.
Odysseus was the king of Ithaca, a small rocky island nobody had much reason to visit.
He wasn't the strongest of the Greeks, or the bravest.
What he had was a mind that never stopped looking for the trick.
His trick was a horse.
A huge wooden one, hollow inside, left in front of the gates as an offering to the gods.
Then the whole Greek army burned its camp and sailed away.
The Trojans came out and found the beach empty.
After ten years, the enemy had simply gone.
So they dragged the horse into the city, and they drank and danced around it, and eventually they went to sleep.
That night a hatch opened in its belly.
Odysseus climbed down a rope with his best men and opened the gates from the inside,
and the army, which had only been hiding behind an island, came back in the dark.
By morning Troy was ash.
The Greeks had won, but they hadn't won cleanly.
They burned temples, and they dragged people away from the altars where they'd gone to beg the gods for help.
The gods saw all of it.
Odysseus loaded his twelve ships with gold and slaves and wine and turned toward home.
Ithaca was a few weeks' sail away.
It took him ten years.
The first place they stopped was a city called Ismarus, which had nothing to do with Troy at all.
Odysseus attacked it anyway.
His men killed the men, took the women, and carried off the wine and the cattle.
It was easy and it was profitable, and when it was done Odysseus told them to get back to the ships.
They didn't listen.
They were drunk on the wine and on how easy it had been, so they stayed on the beach roasting cattle,
and while they ate, the neighbours of the city came down out of the hills.
By the time the ships pushed off, seventy-two of his men were lying dead on the sand.
Six from every ship.
Then a storm caught them.
For nine days the wind dragged them south, off the edge of every map they knew,
and on the tenth day they came to a gentle country where people lived on the fruit of a flower called the lotus.
Odysseus sent three men ashore to say hello.
They didn't come back.
When he went after them, he found them sitting with the Lotus-Eaters, smiling, eating the flower.
Nobody had hurt them and nobody was holding them there.
They just didn't want to go home anymore.
I think that's the strangest danger in the whole story, because you can't fight it.
They had forgotten home existed.
Odysseus dragged them back to the ships in tears, tied them under the rowing benches,
and made everyone else row before anybody else could taste the stuff.
